Sound comes mainly from the bow rubbing the strings, and the strings can be plucked, swept or struck when needed. In the United States a small semicircular bow is common, in Europe a reduced modern violin bow. A beginner should practise single notes first and then try double stops; the strings are close together and not suited to ordinary finger plucking, though they can be lightly plucked at the bowed end.

The player can bow single notes, use two bows at once for double stops, or pluck and strike the strings for other colours. Its main difference from the medieval plucked psaltery is that the strings are laid out for bowing; compared with the violin family it is not stopped, the pitch is fixed by the strings, and the timbre changes with the way the bow is held and the strings are plucked or struck.

The bowed psaltery is a psaltery or zither played with a bow, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-71. Its traditional construction is a wooden soundbox with unfretted strings stretched over it, and the common triangular design gives each string a slightly different length so that each can be bowed on its own; the chromatic instrument puts the sharps and flats on one side and the naturals on the other. It is played with the instrument in one hand and the bow in the other, or laid flat with a bow in each hand, and the strings can be plucked or struck for extra colours. Promoted by German educators after the twentieth century, it was also used in Hawaiian music performances in the United States in the 1920s.
弓形詩篇琴為二十世紀發明。1925年德國克萊門斯·紐伯公司取得專利，加入和弦伴奏: The bowed psaltery was invented in the twentieth century. In 1925 the German firm Clemens Neuber took out a patent, adding chord accompaniment strings so that the melody could be bowed and chords plucked, mostly called the violin zither. In the same period American manufacturers marketed it under Hawaiian-style names such as the ukelin, for the Hawaiian music popular in the 1920s. After the war Walter Mittmann, a primary-school teacher in Westphalia, promoted the triangular form; Edgar Stahmer had earlier argued for its use in education. Today most have no accompaniment strings, though some players retune the chromatic side to make chords.
